home.intro: A channel rack, a piano roll, a playlist and a mixer, and one path from an oscillator through its effect chain to a mixer insert and out the master. Five tabs, ten effects already in the box, and nothing to scan or install before the first note.
home.workflowTitle: Built to stay out of the way
home.workflowBody: Most of what makes a DAW hard to start is not the music. It is forty panels that move, a plugin scan, and a feature set you have to learn before you can hear anything. dew is the other shape: a small, fixed set of screens that always hold the same controls, so the second session works like the first.
home.predictableBody: Five tabs and one instrument panel, in the same places every time. A channel row carries its own volume, pan and on/off; a mixer strip carries its own chain. No modes, no floating windows to lose.
home.signalBody: Three oscillators into an amp envelope, into the channel's effect chain, into a mixer insert, into the master. That is the whole graph, and every knob on it is automatable from its own right-click menu.
home.completeBody: Ten effects, forty factory presets, wavetables, an FM matrix, SoundFont playback and a renderer. Two dependencies in the whole build, no plugin format, and nothing to install per sound.
home.groupsBody: Enough to finish a track, and deliberately not more.
home.openBody: Every line is on GitHub under the AGPLv3 — the application, the audio engine, the score compiler, the tests and this site. Free to use for any purpose, with no warranty of any kind.

mcp.title: Control dew from an agent
mcp.lead: dew runs a Model Context Protocol server inside the application, so a coding agent can read and change the project you have open: instruments, effects, the mixer, the notes and the arrangement.
mcp.howBody: Turn it on under Audio → MCP. dew listens on the loopback interface only. The first time a client connects, dew asks whether to allow it, and whether it may only read or change things too. Every change it makes is one step of your undo history.
mcp.connectBody: The MCP settings panel shows the address and the exact command. The port is not fixed, so copy the command rather than typing it.
mcp.surfaceBody: One address space covers every value in the document. A target, an id, a group and a slot name any parameter of any oscillator, envelope, sample, soundfont, effect, mixer insert or the master. The same four fields say what a curve can be pointed at.
mcp.scoreBody: For anything longer than a few bars, an agent writes dew’s arrangement language and compiles it. The language says what the music is — a key, a progression, rhythms, voicings, a counterpoint — and the compiler works out the notes.

score.title: The score language
score.lead: One of the two ways to write a song in dew: a text description of the whole piece, compiled to real patterns, notes and clips.
score.whatBody: Sketching a whole arrangement faster than you can draw it. You say what the music is — a key, a metre, a progression, a rhythm, a voicing, a melody, a counterpoint answering another voice — and the compiler works out the notes. It is the fifth tab, checked as you type, compiled with ⌘R. The text is stored in the project, so recompiling updates what it wrote last time and leaves anything you have since edited by hand alone.
score.noExpressions: There is no expression language: no arithmetic, no variables, no conditionals. That single restriction is what makes completion a table lookup and lets the grid be worked out before a note is generated.
score.limitsBody: dew stores one tempo and one metre for a whole project, so a section in 3/4 inside a 4/4 project is not expressible. A note’s position is a whole number of steps, so the grid is the least common multiple of what the durations need: sixteenths and eighth-note triplets meet at twelve, and a thirty-second against any triplet is refused.

setup.title: Setup
setup.lead: dew builds from source on macOS, Windows and Linux. Two CMake commands on all three, once the toolchain is there.
setup.presetsBody: release is the one to build for normal use. The first configure fetches JUCE and Catch2 from source, cached per machine under ~/.cache/CPM, so one build is slow and the rest are not.
setup.checkBody: One command, running everything CI runs.
setup.mp3Note: MP3 export needs lame installed separately, in any build: the option stays greyed out until lame is on your PATH. WAV, FLAC and MIDI need nothing.

download.title: Download
download.lead: Builds of dew for macOS, Windows and Linux, from the latest release. It is a working prototype.
download.getBody: Every link points at the latest release. Older versions stay on the releases page.
download.firstRunTitle: The first time you run it
download.firstRunBody: None of these builds is signed. macOS and Windows each block an unsigned application the first time it runs.
download.verifyBody: Every release carries SHA256SUMS.txt, and every asset is covered by a Sigstore build attestation. The attestation records the repository, the workflow and the commit the file was built from.
download.buildBody: Two CMake commands on macOS, Windows and Linux alike. A binary you build yourself is subject to none of the warnings above.
download.mp3Note: MP3 export needs lame installed separately: the option stays greyed out until lame is on your PATH. WAV and FLAC need nothing.
